desc:
A garden bed is a row of plots. bed[i] = 1 means plot i already holds a flower and bed[i] = 0 means it is empty. No two existing flowers are next to each other.

You may plant a new flower in an empty plot only if both neighbouring plots (the ones that exist) are free of flowers, old or newly planted. Return the maximum number of new flowers you can plant.

bed = [1,0,0,0,1]  -> 1
bed = [0,0,0,0,0]  -> 3
bed = [0,0,1,0,0]  -> 2

In the second example, plant at plots 0, 2 and 4.
constraints: The input has no two adjacent 1s
hints: A new flower blocks both of its neighbours. Which plot should you plant in first so that you block as little useful space as possible?
Scan from the left. The leftmost plot you can still plant in is never a worse choice than any plot to its right.
Walk through the plots; whenever a plot is empty and its left neighbour and right neighbour (if they exist) are empty, plant there, count it and mark the plot as occupied.
editorial: Scan left to right and plant a flower in every plot that is currently allowed. Planting in the leftmost allowed plot is safe by an exchange argument: in any optimal answer, the leftmost planted flower can be moved to the leftmost allowed plot without touching anything further right than the plot it blocks, so the count cannot drop.

Mark the plot as occupied as soon as you plant, so the next plot sees the new flower as its left neighbour. Edge plots only check the one neighbour they have. Equivalently, every run of m empty plots between two existing flowers fits (m - 1) // 2 new ones, a run touching one border fits m // 2, and a completely empty bed fits (n + 1) // 2. One pass, O(n).
